19.01.title: Capstone method
19.01.html:
Phase 19 is ten capstone projects in the style of an ETH Fokus-Projekt or Bachelor thesis. Each one pulls several phases together: a fluid solver and a field measurement, a FEM model and a safety factor, a controller and a thermal limit. Before the first one, this lesson sets out the method that turns “I worked on a turbine” into “here is the evidence that it meets its requirements”.

Requirements you can test

A good requirement is specific, measurable and verifiable: “deliver at least 2.0 kW electrical at the design flow”, not “be efficient”. Write each one with an ID, a number and a unit. Then decide how it will be verified:

  • Test: measure it on the built thing.
  • Analysis: compute it with a model you have validated.
  • Inspection: look at it, for example check a weld or a drawing.
  • Demonstration: show it working, for example a fresh clone that rebuilds every figure.

The verification matrix

The verification matrix is a table with one row per requirement and the tests that close it. Two rules make it useful: every requirement has at least one test, and every test traces to a requirement. A requirement without a test is a hope. A test without a requirement is effort that proves nothing anyone asked for. The matrix in the code below fails loudly if either rule breaks, so it can run in continuous integration next to the analysis code.

The critical path

List the tasks with their durations and predecessors. A forward pass gives each task’s earliest start ES=max(EFpred​) and earliest finish EF=ES+d. A backward pass from the end date gives the latest finish LF=min(LSsucc​) and latest start LS=LF−d. The float LS−ES is how far a task can slip without delaying the project. Tasks with zero float form the critical path: any slip on them moves the hand-over date week for week.

Risk

For each risk, score the likelihood L and the impact I on a 1 to 5 scale. The product L×I ranks them. Mitigate the top ones first, and write down the score you expect after mitigation, so that you can check later whether it worked.

Worked examplePlan a micro-hydro capstone

A 2 kW turbine for a village in Bali (lesson 19.05 sizes it).

  1. Requirements. R1: at least 2.0 kW electrical. R2: runner stress below half of yield at runaway speed. R3: the penstock survives the water hammer of a 2 s valve closure. R4: frequency within 50 ± 1 Hz from 20 % to 100 % load. R5: all figures rebuild from a fresh clone in under 10 minutes.
  2. Matrix. Six tests close the five requirements. R1 is closed twice, by a test (2.31 kW) and an analysis (2.42 kW). The code asserts that every requirement has a passing test and every test has a requirement. The measured values here are illustrative: in your project they come from your own lessons and measurements.
  3. Schedule. Nine tasks. The forward and backward passes give 16 weeks. The critical path is A-B-C-E-G-H-I; the penstock design (D) and the pipe and generator purchase (F) have 2 weeks of float each.
  4. Risk. The top risk is a dry-season flow below the design flow (4×4=16). Sizing for the flow exceeded 90 % of the time and measuring in August brings it to 8. The runner casting (12), village interest (10) and a late generator (9) follow.

Exercise 1Find the critical path

Tasks: P (3 weeks), Q (2 weeks, after P), R (4 weeks, after P), S (1 week, after Q and R). How long is the project, which tasks are critical, and how much float does Q have?

Show step-by-step solution
  1. Forward pass: P 0 to 3, Q 3 to 5, R 3 to 7, S starts at max(5,7)=7 and ends at 8. The project takes 8 weeks.
  2. Backward pass: S has LS 7, so R has LF 7 and LS 3, and Q has LF 7 and LS 5.
  3. Critical path P-R-S. Q has 5−3=2 weeks of float.

quiz.q: Earliest finish (weeks) of a 3-week task whose predecessors finish at weeks 4 and 6.
quiz.explain: ES = max(EF of predecessors) = 6, EF = 9.

quiz.q: Float (weeks) of a task with ES = 5 and LS = 8.
quiz.explain: LS − ES.

quiz.q: Risk score for likelihood 3 and impact 5.
quiz.explain: L × I.

quiz.q: A requirement with no test in the verification matrix:
quiz.explain: Every requirement needs evidence.
options: Should be removed from the matrix
Is fine if the design is good
Is unverified, so the project cannot claim it

quiz.q: A one-week slip on a task with two weeks of float:
quiz.explain: It stays within the float, though the task now has only one week left.
options: Delays the project by one week
Makes the task critical with negative float

19.02.title: "Coconut eddy: from field video to CFD"
19.02.html:
Lesson 17.10 asked why a coconut can circle behind a boulder in a Bali river for minutes on end. This capstone closes the loop the way a real study would: measure the coconut’s path from video, model the eddy, and compare the two, explaining whatever does not agree. The scene itself is in the Coconut lab.

The pipeline

  1. Film from a fixed point above the river, with two markers a known distance apart in the frame for the scale (and four for a full perspective correction).
  2. Background. The median of many frames over time is the river without the coconut.
  3. Detect. Subtract the background, blur a little (single bright pixels from sun glints disappear), threshold, and take the intensity-weighted centroid of what remains.
  4. Track. Predict the next position with constant velocity and only search a window around it. If the coconut is lost, search the whole frame again.
  5. Convert pixels to metres and frames to seconds, then compute what the model can predict: the orbit period around the eddy centre and the residence time, the time until the coconut leaves a box 4D long behind the boulder.

The model

The kinematic wake of lesson 17.10: uniform flow U past a cylinder of radius a, with Föppl’s pair of vortices on the curve r−a2/r=2y and their images. The strength that holds the pair stationary is

Γ=4πUy0​(1−r04​a4​).

Real eddies have a finite core, so the point vortex is smoothed with a factor d2/(d2+rc2​) at distance d from the centre. Shedding is modelled by wobbling the two strengths in antiphase at the Strouhal frequency, Γ(1±εsinωt) with ω=2πStU/D.

What to expect

In the steady model the streamlines inside the bubble are closed, so the coconut never leaves. With shedding, fluid crosses the bubble edge in lobes once per cycle and the motion becomes chaotic: two coconuts released 3 cm apart can leave a minute or ten minutes apart. A single measured residence time is therefore one sample from a wide distribution. The fair comparison is: does the measurement fall inside the model’s spread?

Worked exampleTrack it and compare

Honest note: no field footage was available to the machine that built this course, so the “video” is synthetic: 240 s at 10 frames per second and 2 cm per pixel, rendered from the unsteady model with ε=0.22, rc​=0.25 m, a 1 m boulder and U=0.4 m/s, plus water texture, noise and sun glints. The tracking code does not know any of this and would run unchanged on real frames.

  1. Föppl pair. At x0​=1.2 m the curve gives y0​=0.5702 m and Γ=2.809 m²/s. With point vortices the induced velocity at the vortex is zero to 10−3, so the formula holds.
  2. Tracking. The coconut is found in 1822 frames, and it drops fewer than 3 % of frames before it leaves. The median position error is 0.29 cm, under a fifth of a pixel. The worst is 7.3 cm, when the blob overlaps glints.
  3. Measured. The coconut circles the eddy 80.6 times with a mean orbit period of 2.30 s and leaves the 4D box after 185.7 s.
  4. Steady model from the measured release point: orbit period 2.11 s, 8.6 % shorter than measured, and 40 neighbouring release points are all still trapped after 240 s. The steady model gets the circling right and the escape completely wrong.
  5. Unsteady model, 60 release points within the 3 cm tracking uncertainty: 58 % escape within 240 s, and the residence times have 10 %, 50 % and 90 % points of 28.8 s, 154.0 s and more than 240 s. The measured 185.7 s lies inside that range.
  6. Discrepancy explained. The escape comes from the shedding, not from the mean eddy. The orbit period differs because the wobble enlarges the orbits. On a real river, wind on the coconut and its own inertia add further differences, and ε has to come from the CFD of lesson 17.09 or from the eddy’s own wobble in the video.

Exercise 1Plan the field day

You will film from a bridge 6 m above the water with a phone at 30 frames per second and 1920 pixels across a 12 m wide view. The coconut moves at up to 1 m/s. How many pixels is a 15 cm coconut, how far does it move between frames, and how should you size the search window?

Show step-by-step solution
  1. Scale: 12/1920=6.25 mm per pixel, so the coconut spans 24 pixels.
  2. At 1 m/s and 30 fps it moves 33 mm per frame, about 5.3 pixels.
  3. A window of about 3 times the frame-to-frame motion plus the coconut’s radius, roughly 30 pixels, keeps it even when the velocity prediction is off. Fix the phone on a tripod, because camera shake moves everything.

quiz.q: Shedding frequency (Hz) behind a 1.5 m boulder in a 0.6 m/s river, St = 0.2. 2 decimals.
quiz.explain: f=StU/D.

quiz.q: Föppl strength Γ (m²/s) for U = 1 m/s, a = 1 m, y₀ = 1 m, r₀ = 2 m. 4 decimals.
quiz.explain: 4πUy0​(1−a4/r04​).

quiz.q: Scale (mm per pixel) for a 10 m wide view across 2000 pixels. 1 decimal.
A steady recirculation bubble traps a tracer for ever because:
quiz.explain: In steady flow, particle paths are streamlines.

quiz.q: The fair way to compare one measured residence time with a chaotic model is:
quiz.explain: Chaotic advection makes single trajectories unpredictable.
options: Check that it falls inside the model’s spread from nearby release points
Require the model to match it exactly

19.03.title: "Subak weir network: water balance for terraced fields"
19.03.html:
Bali’s subak system has shared river water between rice terraces for about a thousand years. A weir in the river feeds a canal, proportional dividers split the canal between groups of farmers, and the water then steps down from field to field over small outlet weirs. This capstone models a small network for a year and asks the question every farmer asks in August: does the water reach my field? You can explore the real system in the Subak lab.

Weirs

A sharp-crested rectangular weir of width b with head H above the crest passes

Q=32​Cd​b2g​H3/2,

with Cd​≈0.62. A proportional divider puts several notches at the same crest level. They all see the same head, so each passes a flow in proportion to its width, whatever the total:

∑k​Qk​Qi​​=∑k​bk​bi​​.

That is why the subak cuts the notch widths in proportion to each group’s land: the share stays fair in a flood and in a drought.

Water balance of one terrace

Each field of area A holds a ponding depth h. Over a time step Δt,

AΔh=(Qin​−Qout​)Δt+PAΔt−VET​−Vperc​,

where Qout​ is the outlet weir flow with head h−hc​ above the crest hc​, P is rain, and evapotranspiration and percolation take about 5 mm and 3 mm a day. The outflow of one terrace is the inflow of the next one down.

The update is written so that every cubic metre is booked exactly once. Each loss is capped at what the field actually holds, so the depth can never go negative. The test is then strict: the ledger must close at every terrace to rounding error, and the whole network must close as well.

Worked exampleA year on a 1.9 ha network

Three branches of four terraces with 8400, 6600 and 4200 m² of rice. The outlet crests are 5 cm high and 30 cm wide. The river flow, rain and season are assumed, not measured: 60 to 80 L/s in the wet season (November to April) with afternoon showers, and 3 L/s in the dry season. The intake takes half the river, up to 25 L/s.

  1. Divider. Notches of 200, 157.1 and 100 mm. At 6 cm head they pass 5.382, 4.228 and 2.691 L/s, shares of 0.4375, 0.3438 and 0.2188, exactly the land shares.
  2. Mass balance. The worst terrace balance error over the year is about 10−13 of the water that passed through it. The network takes in 438 871 m³ of canal water and rain, and the outflow to the river, the losses and the change in storage add up to the same number.
  3. Dry-season demand. 8 mm/day×19200 m2 is 1.778 L/s, and the intake delivers 1.5 L/s, 84 % of the demand.
  4. Proportional split. The top three terraces of every branch keep standing water all dry season. The tail-end terraces have it only 33 to 35 % of the time, because each field fills to its crest before it passes anything on.
  5. Rotation. Sending the whole flow to one branch for 5 days at a time spreads the shortage: the worst terrace is still near 35 %, but branch 3’s tail-end field rises from 33 % to 65 %. The mean over all fields falls from 0.836 to 0.660, because fields that dry out between turns lose water to re-wetting.

So rotation is fairer to the tail, at a cost in total. In practice the subak’s water temple schedule also staggers planting so that not every field needs full water at once, which this model does not include.

Exercise 1Fill a field

A dry 2000 m² terrace with a 5 cm outlet crest receives 5 L/s from the canal while losing 8 mm a day. How long does it take before water starts to spill to the next field? And once full, how long would it stay wet if the canal stopped?

Show step-by-step solution
  1. Volume to the crest: 2000×0.05=100 m³.
  2. Losses: 0.008×2000/86400=1.85×10−4 m³/s, so the net inflow is 4.815×10−3 m³/s.
  3. Time to fill: 100/4.815×10−3=20770 s, about 5.77 h.
  4. With no inflow the 5 cm lasts 50/8=6.25 days, which is why a 5-day rotation keeps most fields wet.

quiz.q: Flow (m³/s) over a 0.3 m wide sharp-crested weir with 0.1 m head, Cd = 0.62. 5 decimals.
quiz.explain: Q=32​Cd​b2g​H3/2.

quiz.q: A divider serves 8400, 6600 and 4200 m². The first notch is 200 mm. Width (mm) of the second? 4 decimals.
quiz.explain: Widths in proportion to land.

quiz.q: Dry-season demand (L/s) of 19 200 m² of rice losing 8 mm a day. 4 decimals.
quiz.explain: Depth per day times area, divided by 86 400 s.

quiz.q: A proportional divider keeps the share fair at any flow because:
quiz.explain: Same head, so Q is proportional to b.
options: The water speed is the same everywhere
All notches share one crest level and see the same head
The notches are the same width

quiz.q: In a shortage, rotating the whole flow between branches:
quiz.explain: Fields that dry between turns lose water to re-wetting.
options: Helps tail-end fields but lowers the network’s average wetted time
Makes every field wet all the time

19.04.title: "Bamboo footbridge: FEM, statics and the joints"
19.04.html:
A 6 m footbridge over an irrigation canal, built from local bamboo. This capstone sizes it with the direct stiffness method of Phase 10, checks the result two independent ways, and then finds what actually governs. Try breaking a truss first in the Break the bridge lab.

Not a design. The strengths, bolt capacities and safety factors below are assumptions for teaching. Bamboo varies a lot between species, culms and seasons, and it rots and splits. A bridge people walk on needs tested material, a recognised code (for example ISO 22156 for bamboo structures) and a licensed engineer.

The structure

Two Pratt trusses 1 m deep, six 1 m panels, with the deck hung from the bottom chords. Every member is a culm of 80 mm outside diameter and 8 mm wall, so

A=4π​(D2−d2)=1809.6 mm2,I=64π​(D4−d4)=1.187×106 mm4.

With 12 nodes, 21 members and 3 support reactions, m+r=2j: the truss is statically determinate, so the forces do not depend on E and can be checked by hand.

Loads and checks

  • Loads per truss: a crowd of 4 kPa and a deck of 0.6 kPa on a 1.2 m deck, factored by 1.5 and 1.35, so w=4.086 kN/m.
  • Members: axial stress against assumed characteristic strengths of 40 MPa in compression and 80 MPa in tension, divided by 2.
  • Buckling: pin-ended Euler, Pcr​=π2EI/L2, also divided by 2.
  • Joints: a 12 mm bolt through a mortar-filled node, assumed good for 4 kN.
  • Deflection: crowd only, unfactored, against L/250.

Statics gives an independent check at midspan, Nchord​=wL2/(8H). Virtual work, δ=∑Ni​ni​Li​/(EA) with ni​ the forces from a unit load, checks the FEM displacement.

Worked exampleSize the bridge

  1. FEM. The reactions are 12.26 kN at each end, which carries the 24.52 kN total load. The top chord across midspan carries −18.387 kN and the bottom chord +16.344 kN.
  2. Statics. wL2/(8H)=4.086×36/8=18.387 kN, equal to the top chord force to machine precision. A section through the bottom chord panel next to midspan gives 16.344 kN, also exact.
  3. Virtual work. The midspan deflection under the factored load is 7.185 mm by both methods. Under the crowd alone it is 4.22 mm, far inside L/250=24 mm.
  4. Members. The worst member is the top chord at 0.51 utilisation in compression. Buckling of a 1 m panel is only 0.21, and of the 1.41 m end post 0.33.
  5. Joints. With one bolt at each member end, the joint carrying the top chord would be at 4.60, overloaded more than four times. The joints govern by far.
  6. Redesign. Run the chords as continuous culms through the nodes, so a node only carries the web members. The diagonals then need 1 to 3 bolts and the end posts 4, and every check passes.

The lesson from real bamboo structures is the same: the culm is strong, the connection is the problem.

Exercise 1The end post

The end post runs at 45° from the support to the first top node. The support reaction is 12.26 kN and the load at the end node is 2.043 kN. Find the end post force, its stress and its buckling utilisation with a factor of 2, using E=15 GPa.

Show step-by-step solution
  1. Vertical equilibrium at the support node: the post carries 12.26−2.043=10.215 kN vertically, so N=10.2152​=14.446 kN in compression.
  2. Stress: 14446/1809.6=7.98 MPa, against 40/2=20 MPa, a utilisation of 0.40.
  3. Buckling: Pcr​=π2×15×109×1.187×10−6/2=87.9 kN for the 1.414 m post. Divided by 2 that is 43.9 kN, so the utilisation is 0.33.

quiz.q: Area (mm²) of a bamboo culm, 100 mm outside diameter, 10 mm wall. 5 significant figures.
quiz.explain: 4π​(D2−d2).

quiz.q: Midspan chord force (kN) for w = 3 kN/m, L = 8 m, H = 1.2 m. 4 decimals.
quiz.explain: wL2/(8H).

quiz.q: Euler load (kN), pin-ended, E = 15 GPa, I = 1.187e-6 m⁴, L = 2 m. 4 decimals.
quiz.explain: π2EI/L2.

quiz.q: A plane truss with 12 nodes, 21 members and 3 reactions is:
quiz.explain: m+r=24=2j.

quiz.q: In bamboo trusses, what usually governs?
quiz.explain: Bamboo splits at bolts long before the culm fails.

19.05.title: "Micro-hydro: sizing a Pelton turbine"
19.05.html:
A stream drops 40 m over 150 m of hillside above a village. This capstone turns that into electricity: size the penstock, find the net head, then design the nozzle and the Pelton runner so they match a standard 50 Hz generator. It uses the pipe flow of Phase 07 and the turbomachinery of Phase 17.

Penstock and net head

The penstock loses head to friction and fittings,

hf​=(fDL​+∑K)2gV2​,f=[log10​(3.7Dε​+Re0.95.74​)]20.25​,

the explicit Swamee-Jain fit to Colebrook. The net head is Hn​=Hg​−hf​. A bigger pipe loses less head but costs more, so the right diameter balances pipe cost against the value of the energy lost over the scheme’s life.

The jet and the bucket

The nozzle turns the net head into a jet, V=Cv​2gHn​​ with Cv​≈0.97. A bucket moving at speed u sees the jet arrive at the relative speed V−u, turns it through β≈165°, and friction keeps a fraction k of the relative speed. The force times the bucket speed gives the Euler turbine equation

P=ρQu(V−u)(1−kcosβ),

which peaks at u=V/2 with hydraulic efficiency η=(1+kcos15°)/2. The jet’s kinetic power splits exactly into shaft power, the kinetic energy that leaves the bucket, and the bucket friction loss, and the code checks that balance at every speed.

Worked exampleDesign the scheme

Assumed site: 40 m gross head, 20 L/s, 150 m of HDPE penstock (ε=0.007 mm) with fittings ∑K=1.5. The assumed set efficiency is 0.972×0.935×0.95×0.90=0.752: nozzle, runner, belt and bearings, generator.

  1. Penstock. A 90 mm pipe loses 13.65 m and a 200 mm pipe 0.30 m. With pipe at about 18 EUR per metre for 100 mm (scaling as D1.6) and energy at 0.10 EUR/kWh for 10 years at 70 % capacity factor, 125 mm is cheapest at about 6390 EUR, just ahead of 160 mm at about 6510 EUR. It loses 2.80 m, 7.0 % of the gross head, inside the usual 10 % rule.
  2. Check. Swamee-Jain matches an iterated Colebrook friction factor within 2 % at Re=2.04×105.
  3. Jet. Hn​=37.20 m, so V=0.972×9.81×37.20​=26.206 m/s.
  4. Runner. The Euler power peaks at u/V=0.500 with η=0.9347, exactly (1+0.9cos15°)/2. Real runners run nearer u/V=0.46, where the ideal efficiency is still 0.929.
  5. Matching the generator. At u=0.46V and 1500 rpm the pitch diameter would be only 153 mm against a 31.2 mm jet, a ratio of 4.9. Buckets need a pitch diameter of at least about 10 jet diameters. Two jets of 22.0 mm and a runner at 1000 rpm, belted up to a 1500 rpm 4-pole generator, give a 230 mm runner and a ratio of 10.4.
  6. Output. P=ηρgQHn​=5.49 kW electric, enough for the lights, phones and a rice huller of a small village.

Exercise 1The dry season

In the dry season the stream gives only 8 L/s. Keep the 125 mm penstock and assume the set efficiency stays at 0.752. What is the head loss, the power, and what should the operator do with the two jets?

Show step-by-step solution
  1. Velocity V=0.008/(π×0.1252/4)=0.652 m/s, Re=8.1×104, and Swamee-Jain gives f≈0.0189.
  2. hf​=(0.0189×1200+1.5)×0.6522/19.62=0.52 m, so Hn​≈39.5 m.
  3. P=0.752×9810×0.008×39.5=2.33 kW.
  4. The jet speed depends on head, not flow, so the right move is to shut one jet and keep the other spear valve near its best opening. A Pelton’s efficiency stays high at part flow this way, which is one reason Peltons suit village hydro.

quiz.q: Jet velocity (m/s) for a net head of 50 m, Cv = 0.97. 4 decimals.
quiz.explain: Cv​2gHn​​.

quiz.q: Peak hydraulic efficiency for k = 0.85 and a 165° bucket. 4 decimals.
quiz.explain: (1+kcos15°)/2.

quiz.q: Pitch diameter (m) for a bucket speed of 15 m/s at 1000 rpm. 5 significant figures.
quiz.explain: D=60u/(πN).

quiz.q: Why is the ideal bucket speed half the jet speed?
quiz.explain: Maximise u(V−u).
options: Power is u(V − u), which peaks at u = V/2

quiz.q: A larger penstock diameter:
quiz.explain: The best diameter balances pipe cost against lost energy.
options: Increases the jet velocity without limit
Costs more but loses less head

19.06.title: "Pumped storage: energy balance and water hammer"
19.06.html:
A village solar grid makes too much power at noon and none in the evening. This capstone stores the surplus by pumping water 50 m up a hill into a tank and runs it back through a turbine after dark. Two things matter: an energy ledger that accounts for every kilowatt-hour, and the pressure surge when a valve in the 300 m penstock closes.

The energy ledger

Pumping a flow Q against the static head Hs​ through a pipe with friction head kf​Q2 needs hydraulic power ρgQ(Hs​+kf​Q2). Generating gives ρgQ(Hs​−kf​Q2). Every joule of solar surplus ends up in one of: the evening load, the pump and turbine losses, pipe friction, or potential energy in the tank,

Ein​=Eout​+Epump loss​+Eturbine loss​+Efriction​+ΔEp​.

The code evaluates the head at the middle of each step’s slab of water, ρgAΔz(z0​+z+Δz/2), so the potential energy of a prism is exact and the ledger closes to rounding error. The round-trip efficiency is

ηrt​=ηp​ηt​Hs​+hf,p​Hs​−hf,t​​.

Water hammer

Stopping a flow suddenly sends a pressure wave up the pipe at the wave speed

a=1+KD/(Ee)K/ρ​​,

where K is the water’s bulk modulus and the pipe wall of thickness e and modulus E stretches a little. The rise for a sudden stop is Joukowsky’s ΔH=aΔV/g. Any closure faster than the round trip 2L/a counts as sudden. Slower closures let the reflected wave relieve the valve, and Michaud’s estimate is ΔH≈2LV/(gTc​). The method of characteristics solves the full wave equations along the lines dx/dt=±a, with the reservoir and the closing valve as boundaries.

Worked exampleA day of storage and a valve closure

Assumed: tank floor 50 m above the pond, 2000 m² tank, 300 m steel penstock of 300 mm with f=0.015, pump 78 % and turbine 82 % efficient including their electric machines. Solar surplus up to 40 kW from 08:00 to 16:00, and a 15 kW evening load from 18:00 to 23:00.

  1. Ledger. 241.978 kWh in. 75.000 kWh out to the village, 53.235 kWh pump losses, 16.463 kWh turbine losses, 1.830 kWh pipe friction, and 95.450 kWh left in the tank. The sum matches the input to 10−15.
  2. Levels. The tank rises from 1.000 m to 1.669 m and ends the night at 1.342 m, so the evening demand is fully served and the tank is more than big enough.
  3. Round trip. At mid level, pumping 30 kW lifts 45.6 L/s with 0.318 m of friction, and generating 15 kW takes 36.0 L/s with 0.198 m. The round-trip efficiency is 0.6333, barely below the machines' 0.6396: in a pipe this size, friction hardly matters.
  4. Wave speed. A 6 mm steel wall gives a=1191.4 m/s and 2L/a=0.504 s.
  5. Joukowsky. The generating flow moves at 0.509 m/s, so a sudden stop adds aV/g=61.85 m, more than doubling the head. The MOC gives 62.04 m for an instant closure and 61.96 m for a 0.504 s closure.
  6. Slow closure. Closing over 10 s keeps the rise to 2.00 m, 3 % of the sudden surge. Michaud predicts 3.11 m, so here it is conservative, because with a linear closure the flow falls mostly at the end. The penstock must still be rated for about 114 m, in case a valve is slammed or the power fails and the guide vanes trip.

Exercise 1HDPE instead of steel

Replace the steel penstock with HDPE of 300 mm and 18 mm wall, E=1.0 GPa. Find the wave speed, 2L/a and the Joukowsky rise for V=0.509 m/s. Which pipe is kinder to the valve, and what is the catch?

Show step-by-step solution
  1. The wall term is
EeKD​=1.0×109×0.0182.2×109×0.3​=36.7.
  1. a=2.2×106/37.7​=241.6 m/s, and 2L/a=2.48 s.
  2. ΔH=241.6×0.509/9.81=12.5 m, about a fifth of the steel value.
  3. HDPE is kinder to the valve, because the flexible wall absorbs the surge. The catch is that it is weaker and creeps, so its pressure rating at 114 m is far harder to meet, and it must be buried or shaded from the sun.

quiz.q: Wave speed (m/s) in a rigid pipe, K = 2.2 GPa, ρ = 1000 kg/m³. 4 decimals.
quiz.explain: a=K/ρ​ with a rigid wall.

19.07.title: "E-bike drivetrain: gear ratio, energy and heat"
19.07.html:
An e-bike for the hills of Bali has to do two things that pull against each other: reach the 25 km/h assist limit on the flat, and climb long 8 % roads without cooking its motor. This capstone sizes the gear ratio of a mid-drive using the DC motor of Phase 14, the vehicle dynamics of Phase 06 and the thermal RC model of Phase 08.

Motor and road

A brushed or field-oriented brushless motor behaves as

V=Kωm​+IR,τm​=KI,

with the same constant K for back-EMF and torque in SI units. The controller limits the current to Imax​, and it cannot push more current than the back-EMF leaves room for. Through a reduction G with efficiency ηg​, the wheel of radius r gets

Fw​=rηg​GKI​+vPrider​​,ωm​=rGv​.

The road takes Fr​=mg(Crr​cosθ+sinθ)+21​ρCd​Av2. A tall gear (small G) spins the motor slowly and gives a high top speed but little force; a low gear (large G) climbs well but runs out of back-EMF headroom before 25 km/h.

Heat

On a long climb at the current limit, the copper loss I2R heats the winding through a thermal RC,

Cth​dtdT​=I2R−Rth​T−Tamb​​,

which tends to Tamb​+I2RRth​ with time constant Rth​Cth​. A slow climb lasts many time constants and gets there.

Energy ledger

With ideal PWM the battery supplies (Kωm​+IR)I. That plus the rider’s work goes into copper loss, gear loss, rolling and air drag, potential energy and kinetic energy. Booking every force at the step’s mid-speed makes the work equal the change in kinetic energy, and the ledger closes up to the time-step error.

Worked exampleChoose the ratio

Assumed: 100 kg of bike and rider, Crr​=0.008, Cd​A=0.55 m², 0.35 m wheel, a 36 V motor with R=0.25 Ω and K=0.08 N m/A, 15 A limit, ηg​=0.92, a rider giving 100 W, and a winding with Cth​=400 J/K and Rth​=1.8 K/W in 30 °C air. The test climb is 3 km at 8 %, 240 m up.

Ratio Flat, km/h On 8 %, km/h Climb time Winding peak Battery
10 25.0 6.5 27.8 min 121.3 °C 54.6 Wh
16 25.0 9.5 19.0 min 110.4 °C 63.5 Wh
22 25.0 15.7 11.6 min 92.6 °C 73.7 Wh
26 21.7 19.7 9.3 min 78.7 °C 78.1 Wh
  1. Ratio 10 creeps up the hill at the current limit for 27.8 minutes, nearly three thermal time constants of 720 s. The winding reaches 121.3 °C, over its 120 °C limit, although it uses the least battery.
  2. Ratio 26 climbs fastest and coolest, but its no-load speed is below 25 km/h, so it never reaches the assist limit on the flat.
  3. Ratio 22 is the largest that still reaches 25.0 km/h: the motor’s no-load speed of V/K=450 rad/s maps to 25.8 km/h at the wheel. It climbs at 15.7 km/h and peaks at 92.6 °C.
  4. Check at 15.7 km/h. The motor gives 0.92×22×0.08×15/0.35=69.4 N and the rider 22.9 N, against 86.05 N of grade and rolling plus 6.2 N of drag.
  5. Ledger for ratio 22. 73.69 Wh from the battery and 19.26 Wh from the rider go into 10.83 Wh copper, 5.03 Wh gear, 11.63 Wh rolling and drag, 65.19 Wh potential energy and 0.26 Wh kinetic energy. The relative mismatch is 4×10−6, the time-step error.
  6. Range. The climb uses 24.6 Wh/km, so a 500 Wh pack covers about 20 km of it.

Exercise 1Steady winding temperature

On the ratio 10 climb the motor sits at the 15 A limit. Find the copper loss, the steady winding temperature, and the time constant. How long would the climb have to be for the winding to stay under 120 °C?

Show step-by-step solution
  1. Copper loss 152×0.25=56.25 W.
  2. Steady temperature 30+56.25×1.8=131.3 °C, over the limit.
  3. Time constant Rth​Cth​=720 s.
  4. From T=T∞​−(T∞​−T0​)e−t/τ with T0​=30 °C: e−t/720=11.25/101.25, so t=720ln9=1582 s, about 26 minutes. The 27.8 minute climb is just too long, which matches the simulation.

quiz.explain: At zero current V=Kω.

quiz.q: Wheel speed (km/h) at a motor speed of 400 rad/s, G = 20, wheel radius 0.34 m. 4 decimals.
quiz.explain: v=ωm​r/G.

quiz.q: Grade plus rolling force (N), 90 kg, Crr 0.01, 10 % grade. 5 significant figures.
quiz.explain: mg(Crr​cosθ+sinθ) with θ=arctan0.1.

quiz.q: Raising the reduction ratio G:
quiz.explain: Torque multiplied, speed divided.
options: Increases hill force but lowers the top speed

quiz.q: Why is a slow climb hard on the motor?
quiz.explain: Copper loss I2R at the limit for a long time.
options: It sits at the current limit for many thermal time constants

19.08.title: "Flywheel store: stresses and the burst margin"
19.08.html:
Clouds over a village solar grid can drop the output for half a minute at a time. A steel flywheel can carry the load through: it spins up on surplus and gives the energy back through a motor-generator. This capstone sizes the wheel and then asks the safety question first: how far is it from bursting? Spin one up in the Spinning flywheel lab.

Energy

A disc of radius b, thickness t and density ρ has I=21​ρπb4t and stores 21​Iω2. Running between ωmax​ and ωmax​/2 releases 75 % of it. Per kilogram a flat disc stores

mE​=4(ωb)2​,

so the rim speed sets the specific energy, not the size.

Stresses in a rotating disc

Radial equilibrium of a thin disc in plane stress leads to

dr2d2u​+r1​drdu​−r2u​=−E(1−ν2)ρω2r​,

with σr​=0 at free edges. For a solid disc the closed form peaks at the centre,

σr​=σθ​=83+ν​ρω2b2.

A bore, however small, makes the hoop stress at its edge

σθ​(a)=43+ν​ρω2(b2+3+ν1−ν​a2),

about twice the solid value. All stresses grow as ω2, so the disc bursts at ωmax​σu​/σmax​​. The code solves the equation by finite differences and checks it against both closed forms.

Worked exampleSize and check the wheel

Assumed: 4340 steel, ρ=7850 kg/m³, ν=0.29, yield 860 MPa, ultimate 1000 MPa. The wheel must give 10 kW for 30 s, 300 kJ usable, and has a 0.30 m radius.

  1. Stress-limited speed. Putting half of yield at the centre gives 11 617 rpm, a 365 m/s rim and a disc only 5.4 mm thick weighing 12.0 kg at 33.30 kJ/kg. In air that is a saw blade, not an energy store: drag, balance and the bearings rule it out.
  2. Rim-speed-limited. At 150 m/s the wheel runs at 4775 rpm. With I=300000/(0.5×5002×0.75)=3.2 kg m², it is 32.0 mm thick, weighs 71.1 kg and stores 5.625 kJ/kg, exactly 1502/4 J/kg.
  3. Centre stress. Finite differences give 72.637 MPa, the closed form 72.637 MPa. The yield margin is 11.84 and the disc would burst at 3.710 times full speed, 17 716 rpm.
  4. The bore. With a 40 mm bore the hoop stress at the bore is 145.44 MPa (closed form 145.41), 2.002 times the solid value. The burst speed falls to 2.622 times full speed, 12 520 rpm.
  5. Overspeed. A governor trip at 1.15 times full speed puts 192.3 MPa at the bore, still 4.47 times below yield.
  6. Containment. At full speed the wheel holds 400 kJ, about the kinetic energy of a 1 t car at 100 km/h (386 kJ). The margins above are about stress; a real installation still needs a steel or concrete pit, because a crack, a bad weld or a bearing seizure does not read the margin.

Exercise 1An aluminium wheel

Make the same 0.30 m wheel from 7075-T6 aluminium (ρ=2810 kg/m³, ν=0.33, yield 500 MPa) at the same 150 m/s rim speed with a 40 mm bore. Find the bore hoop stress, the yield margin, and the mass for 300 kJ usable.

Show step-by-step solution
  1. ω=500 rad/s. The bore stress is
σθ​(a)=43.33​×2810×5002(0.09+3.330.67​×0.0004)=52.7 MPa.
  1. Yield margin 500/52.7=9.5.
  2. Specific energy depends only on the rim speed, 5.625 kJ/kg, so the full 400 kJ again needs about 71 kg of metal. Aluminium is lighter per cubic metre, so the disc is 2.8 times thicker, about 89 mm, for the same mass. Its advantage would only show at a higher rim speed, which this design rules out.

quiz.explain: 83+ν​ρ(ωb)2.

quiz.q: Specific energy (kJ/kg) of a flat disc at a 120 m/s rim. 4 decimals.
quiz.explain: (ωb)2/4.

quiz.q: Burst speed as a multiple of full speed, if the peak stress is 160 MPa and the ultimate is 1000 MPa. 4 decimals.
quiz.explain: Stress grows as ω2.

quiz.q: A small central bore in a rotating disc:
quiz.explain: σθ​(a)→43+ν​ρω2b2 as a→0.

About doubles the peak hoop stress

19.09.title: "Wind-loaded sign: gusts, vortices and fatigue"
19.09.html:
A 2 m by 1 m sign on a steel pole by a Bali road looks like the easiest structure in this course. It is a good last design problem because the obvious check, the storm gust, is not the one that breaks it. This capstone uses the beam theory of Phase 04, the vibration of Phase 09 and the fatigue of Phase 11.

Static gust

The drag on the sign is F=21​ρCd​AV2 with Cd​≈1.2 for a flat plate. With the wind on the pole itself, the base moment gives the bending stress σ=M/W with W=I/(D/2) for the tube.

Natural frequency

The pole is a cantilever with the sign as a tip mass. Rayleigh’s method gives

fn​=2π1​msign​+0.236mpole​3EI/L3​​,

checked against a beam finite-element model with cubic Hermite elements.

Two kinds of fatigue

Buffeting. Gusts push the sign back and forth along the wind. The base stress history is counted with rainflow (ASTM E1049), the code checks itself against the standard’s example, and each wind speed bin is weighted by the hours a Weibull wind climate spends there. Miner’s rule adds the damage, D=∑ni​/Ni​.

Vortex shedding. Vortices peel off the round pole at f=StV/D with St≈0.2. When that matches fn​, the pole locks in and vibrates across the wind. The amplitude depends on the Scruton number, damping times mass,

Sc=ρD22δme​​,Dymax​​≈St2ScKKw​clat​​,

where δ is the logarithmic decrement. Bare welded steel has very little damping, δ≈0.012.

Worked exampleCheck the sign

Assumed: pole CHS 168.3 × 5 mm, S355, 4.5 m to the sign centre, 35 kg sign, 35 m/s design gust, Weibull wind with k=2 and c=5.5 m/s, turbulence intensity 0.18, base detail category 71 with γMf​=1.35.

  1. Gust. I=855.8 cm⁴ and W=101.7 cm³. The 35 m/s gust gives 86.7 MPa at the base. After 1.5 on the load and 1.1 on the steel there is still a factor of 2.48. Static strength is not a problem.
  2. Frequency. Rayleigh gives 5.156 Hz and the beam FEM 5.146 Hz, 0.2 % apart.
  3. Rainflow check. The ASTM example gives half a cycle of range 3, one and a half of 4, half of 6, one of 8 and half of 9, exactly the standard’s answer.
  4. Buffeting. Each hour of wind has about 3600 stress cycles. Below 12 m/s mean wind every range is under the cut-off and does no damage. The total is 4.3×10−5 per year, a life of over 20 000 years.
  5. Vortices. Lock-in on the pole is at fn​D/0.2=4.33 m/s, a gentle breeze that blows 1164 hours a year within 10 % of it. With δ=0.012, Sc=37.5 and the tip swings 6.13 mm, a base stress range of 32.09 MPa at 5.15 Hz. That is 2.16×107 cycles a year above the cut-off: a life of about 0.6 years.
  6. Fix. A hanging chain damper or a small tuned mass damper raising δ to 0.15 gives Sc=468.6, a 0.49 mm amplitude and a 2.57 MPa range, below the cut-off. Helical strakes on the pole, or a pole whose frequency puts lock-in well above the common winds, also work.

This simplified Eurocode 1 estimate is conservative: the sign plate adds some aerodynamic damping, and turbulence breaks up lock-in. Cracked base welds on sign and signal poles from wind-induced vibration in light winds are a well-documented failure, though, which is why fatigue at lock-in, not the storm, governs.

Exercise 1Move the lock-in speed

Keep the 4.5 m pole and the 35 kg sign but use a 219.1 × 6.3 mm tube. Estimate the new frequency by scaling fn​∝EI/m​ (ignore the extra pole mass), and the new lock-in speed. Is that better?

Show step-by-step solution
  1. I=64π​(0.21914−0.20654)=2.386×10−5 m⁴, 2.79 times the 168.3 mm tube.
  2. fn​≈5.152.79​=8.6 Hz.
  3. Lock-in =8.6×0.2191/0.2=9.4 m/s, more than twice as high. That wind blows about half as often (about 560 hours a year within 10 %, against 1164 at 4.33 m/s), and the stiffer, heavier pole has a larger Scruton number. Raising the lock-in speed out of the common winds is the classic fix, with dampers for the poles that cannot be changed.

quiz.explain: Amplitude is inversely proportional to the Scruton number.

19.10.title: "Publish: a project anyone can reproduce"
19.10.html:
The last capstone is not a machine but the habit that makes all the others worth something: publish the work so that a stranger can clone it, run it, and get the same numbers. This lesson builds the tool for checking that, SHA-256, from scratch, and uses it on a small project and on this course itself.

What to publish

  1. The source, with a README that says how to run everything in one command, and a licence.
  2. Pinned versions of the language and libraries, because results can shift between versions.
  3. Fixed seeds for anything random, and no time stamps or machine paths in the outputs.
  4. Rounded output. Print results to the precision you actually claim. Floating-point noise in the 16th digit then never reaches the file.
  5. Tests: the asserts in every script of this course are the claims, checked on every run.
  6. A manifest of the SHA-256 hash of every output file, so a reader can check the whole result in one comparison.
  7. Provenance for any data, and an archived release (for example with a DOI) so that the version cited in a report never changes.

SHA-256

A cryptographic hash turns any file into 256 bits. Changing a single bit of the input flips about half of the output bits, and no one knows how to find two inputs with the same hash. So equal hashes mean equal files. The algorithm pads the message to a multiple of 512 bits, then mixes each block into eight 32-bit words over 64 rounds of rotations, additions and bitwise choices,

T1​=h+Σ1​(e)+Ch(e,f,g)+Ki​+Wi​,T2​=Σ0​(a)+Maj(a,b,c),

with Σ1​(e)=(e⋙6)⊕(e⋙11)⊕(e⋙25) and similar for Σ0​. The certificates of this course are checked with the same function.

Worked exampleReproduce from a fresh copy

  1. SHA-256 check. The from-scratch code gives ba7816bf…20015ad for “abc”, the FIPS 180-2 test vector, and matches Python’s hashlib on messages of 0, 55, 56, 64, 119 and 1000 bytes, the padding edge cases.
  2. A small project with three scripts: a deterministic stress check, a Monte Carlo with a fixed seed, and a careless script that prints a time stamp and uses an unseeded generator. The author’s run writes a MANIFEST.sha256.
  3. Two fresh copies of only the source, with no output folder, are built from scratch. The stress check and the seeded Monte Carlo match the manifest in both copies. The careless script differs in both, as it must.
  4. The results themselves: I=8.558456×10−6 m⁴, a base stress of 57.3424 MPa, and P(V>15 m/s)=0.00063 from 200 000 samples against the exact Weibull value 0.00059.
  5. This course. A fresh git clone of the repository at commit fa92b30, with numpy 2.5.4, ran five of the Phase 19 scripts twice each. Every run gave the same hash, equal to the hash from the author’s working copy. For example, the bamboo bridge output hashes to b851d594f284a936… and the Pelton output to cdfe772be2c6df65….

To check this course yourself:

Exercise 1Why the Monte Carlo can still break

The seeded Monte Carlo matched in both fresh copies. Name two changes that could still make a reader’s hash differ, and what you would publish to prevent each.

Show step-by-step solution
  1. A different library version. numpy does not promise the same random stream from default_rng across all versions, and maths library changes can move the last digits of a result. Publish the exact versions, for example a requirements.txt with numpy==2.5.4, or a container image.
  2. Printing too many digits. The 5-decimal probability is safe, but printing a mean to 17 significant figures would expose differences in summation order between machines. Print only the digits you claim.
  3. Other good answers: different line endings on Windows (write files with newline='\n'), or a locale that prints a decimal comma.

quiz.q: How many 512-bit blocks does SHA-256 process for a 100-byte message? 4 decimals.
quiz.explain: The message, one 1 bit and the 64-bit length must fit: 865 bits need 2 blocks.

quiz.q: How many hex characters is a SHA-256 hash? 4 decimals.
quiz.explain: 4 bits per hex character.

quiz.q: About how many output bits flip on average when one input bit changes? 4 decimals.
quiz.explain: The avalanche effect: half of 256.

quiz.q: A script prints a time stamp in its output. Its hash in the manifest:
quiz.explain: The output changes every run.
options: Is reproduced if the seed is fixed
Is reproduced on the same machine

quiz.q: The most robust way to make float results hash the same on every machine:
quiz.explain: Rounding hides last-digit noise.
options: Print them to the precision you claim
